title: How Autoresearch is changing ML research — Zhengyao Jiang, Weco
talk_summary: Weco's Aiden, a multi-agent autoresearch system, ran 1,300 experiments over 22 days on one H100 node in OpenAI's Parameter Golf competition, setting 7 leaderboard records with ~6x the community hit rate while using only 4% of total compute. The speaker's core lesson is that the leverage comes not from brute-force parallelism but from a tight quality gate before publishing, a well-designed eval (loss function) and codebase abstraction (architecture) that bias the agent's search, and agents that mine noisy public channels for implementable ideas.

takeaways.what_they_do: Aiden only submits a PR once findings pass an explicit quality gate, which the speaker credits for lifting signal-to-noise in the community's PR channel.
takeaways.evidence_quote: submit a PR once the findings pass a quality gate
takeaways.numbers: 28% of submissions made leaderboard vs ~6x community average hit rate

takeaways.what_they_do: They frame the eval as the loss function/data and the codebase API abstraction as the architecture, deliberately tightening the abstraction so the agent cannot reward-hack (test data leakage dropped to zero).
takeaways.evidence_quote: a good abstraction leads to better solutions. Even though if the agent really want they can steer reward hack.
takeaways.numbers: data leakage rate dropped to zero after tightening API

takeaways.technique: Mine noisy public channels for implementable ideas
takeaways.what_they_do: Aiden's wins mostly came from finding ideas humans abandoned for implementation difficulty (papers, notes, other PRs) and combining them, not from original invention.
takeaways.numbers: 7 leaderboard records, H-index 10 vs 7 for best human

takeaways.what_they_do: Despite autoresearch's parallelism potential, Aiden ran ~1,300 experiments serially on a single H100 node and won on hit rate, not fan-out.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It didn't win through massive paralization even though auto research have a tons of a potential of paralyzation.
takeaways.numbers: 1,300 experiments / 22 days on one H100; 4% of total compute, 15% of records

takeaways.what_they_do: Aiden's big win came from recognizing a tokenizer improvement posted by another contributor and combining it with its own architectural work after ~5 days of iteration.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Aiden recognized the idea, combine it with architectural work. It just work for five days or so.
takeaways.numbers: three combined ideas produced a large performance jump / leaderboard record

takeaways.technique: Move humans up the stack to eval/abstraction design
takeaways.what_they_do: The speaker argues the durable human skill is designing the eval and codebase abstraction the agent climbs, not doing the execution itself.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Creativity, the judgment to design a good eval or an abstraction. Those will soon get exponentially more important.
